passage:
On the local bus back from the kasba school, a group of Class 11 boys snatched Lalit's cap and tossed it out of the window, laughing at his thin arms. Chaitanya, two seats ahead, kept his eyes on the fields.
Later, at the tea stall where the bus stopped, Chaitanya told his cousin, "Lalit brings it on himself. He talks back. If he kept quiet they'd leave him alone."
"He only asked for his cap," his cousin said.
Chaitanya kicked a stone. If it was Lalit's fault, it could never happen to him.
That evening Lalit told his mother. She sat with him, told him it was not his fault, and walked with him straight to the headmaster's house. The headmaster listened, promised to call the boys' parents, and said he would ride the bus himself the next morning.

qa.q: What did the Class 11 boys do with Lalit's cap?
qa.a: They snatched Lalit's cap and tossed it out of the window.

qa.q: Why does it feel reasonable to Chaitanya to say Lalit 'brings it on himself'?
qa.a: If Lalit caused it, then Chaitanya, who keeps quiet, can feel safe from the same boys; blaming Lalit is more comfortable than admitting he could be next.

qa.q: On the bus, Chaitanya chose to watch the fields. What different choice could he have made?
qa.a: He could have picked up the cap at the next stop or sat beside Lalit, and later told a teacher what he saw.

qa.q: What would change for Lalit if Chaitanya told the headmaster what he saw?
qa.a: Lalit would know someone on the bus saw it as unfair, and the headmaster would have a second account, making it easier to stop the boys.

grounding: A village teen blames a bullied classmate for provoking it so he can feel safe from the same bullies.

passage:
In Aarhus, the Monday class chat was full of Selin's news: her backpack had been taken from the train platform while she tied her shoe. Her laptop and her sketchbook, gone. Her mum had gone with her to report it at the station office that same afternoon.
At lunch Lars shook his head. "Who puts a bag down at a station? Honestly, that's on her."
Freya frowned. "She put it down for ten seconds."
"Then she was careless for ten seconds." Lars said it fast, like closing a door. He took the same platform every morning, his own bag always at his feet. He liked the idea that careful people stay safe.
Selin walked past their table. Lars suddenly became very interested in his sandwich.

qa.q: Where was Selin's backpack taken from?
qa.a: Her backpack was taken from the train platform.

qa.q: What does it mean that Lars 'liked the idea that careful people stay safe'?
qa.a: Lars uses the same platform daily, so blaming Selin lets him believe his own care will protect him, which feels calmer than accepting it could happen to anyone.

qa.q: When Selin walked past, what choice could Lars have made instead of staring at his sandwich?
qa.a: He could have said he was sorry about the bag, which would ease the moment and quietly undo his harsh words.

qa.q: Why might Freya react differently from Lars?
qa.a: Freya seems to imagine being in Selin's place for those ten seconds, so to Freya it looks like bad luck rather than carelessness.

grounding: A teenage boy blames a classmate whose bag was stolen so he can keep feeling safe on the same platform.

passage:
In the boys' hostel common room at the coaching centre, the news was everywhere by dinner: someone had taken Faizan's new cycle from outside the library.
Mohit, sixteen, shrugged over his dal. "He left it with a cheap lock. What did he expect? If you show off a new cycle, you're asking for it."
Sudha ma'am, the warden, was passing with the attendance register. She stopped. "Your cycle is outside the same library, Mohit. What lock does it have?"
Mohit paused. "The same kind, ma'am. But mine's old."
"So if it were stolen tomorrow, would you have asked for it?"
He opened his mouth and shut it again. Blaming Faizan had felt so much safer; if it was Faizan's fault, it couldn't happen to him.
Sudha ma'am said quietly, "The one who took it is responsible. Faizan's just the one who lost it." Then she went to find Faizan, who hadn't come down for dinner.

qa.q: Where was Faizan's cycle taken from?
qa.a: From outside the library.

qa.q: Why did blaming Faizan feel comfortable to Mohit?
qa.a: If the theft was Faizan's fault for showing off, then Mohit could believe it wouldn't happen to him, even though his own cycle had the same kind of lock.

qa.q: What question from Sudha ma'am made Mohit stop, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked whether he would have 'asked for it' if his own cycle were stolen tomorrow, which made him see his reasoning only protected himself.

qa.q: How might Faizan be feeling while the others discuss his cycle at dinner?
qa.a: Faizan, who hadn't come down, is likely upset and perhaps embarrassed, and hearing he 'asked for it' would add shame to the loss.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy blaming a classmate for a theft, a belief that protects his own sense of being safe, and a warden gently challenging it.

passage:
Dear Mehak didi,
Something happened in class that I keep thinking about. For two weeks some boys have been posting mean jokes about Sonali in the class group: about her voice, her glasses. Yesterday she didn't come to school.
When people talked about it at break, I said, "She should just stop answering every question. She kind of brings it on herself." A few boys laughed. I felt clever for about a minute.
Then last night I remembered Class 6, when they made fun of my stammer. I didn't bring that on myself either. I think I said it because if it's her fault, then it won't happen to me again. That's not true, is it?
Today I told our class teacher about the posts. She said she was glad I did and that she'd talk to the school counsellor this afternoon. I don't know what to say to Sonali yet.
Your brother,
Aniket

qa.q: What were the boys posting jokes about?
qa.a: About Sonali's voice and her glasses.

qa.q: How does Aniket feel about what he said at break, and why does he think he said it?
qa.a: Aniket feels ashamed and uneasy, realising that blaming Sonali let him feel safe from being mocked again, the way he was for his stammer in Class 6.

qa.q: What did Aniket do today, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: He told the class teacher about the posts, which brought in an adult who promised to involve the school counsellor that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt reading two weeks of those posts?
qa.a: Sonali probably felt hurt and alone, which may be why she stayed away from school, and hearing classmates blame her would add shame to that hurt.

grounding: A teenage boy's letter shows him blaming a bullied classmate to feel safe himself, then recognising it and telling a teacher.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10A, Tuesday
This morning Kavitha told me that a group from another section has been posting mean edited photos of her. I reported it to the school counsellor within the hour, and Kavitha is meeting the counsellor with her parents this afternoon. In class, I overheard Chaitanya telling his friends, "She must have done something to start it. Nobody gets targeted for no reason." When I asked him privately what he meant, he said, "If you keep quiet and don't show off, nobody bothers you." I think he believes this keeps him safe. I explained that people are targeted for all sorts of reasons, and that blaming Kavitha hurts her twice. He looked uncomfortable and said he hadn't thought of it that way. I will run a session on online bullying with the class on Thursday.

qa.q: Who did the teacher report Kavitha's bullying to?
qa.a: The school counsellor, within the hour.

qa.q: Why does Chaitanya believe Kavitha must have started it?
qa.a: He wants to feel safe, so believing that quiet people are never targeted is comforting, even though it blames Kavitha.

qa.q: What did the teacher do for both students?
qa.a: Reported Kavitha's bullying to the counsellor straight away, and privately explained to Chaitanya that blaming her hurts her twice.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel if she heard Chaitanya's comment?
qa.a: She would likely feel hurt again and more alone, as if the bullying were her fault.

grounding: A teacher records a teenage boy blaming a bullied classmate for provoking it, a belief that helps him feel safe.

passage:
Wednesday
Sonali's phone got snatched at the bus stop yesterday. Two guys on a bike. Everyone was being nice to her today, but honestly, what did she expect? She always has it out, scrolling, not looking around. I keep mine in my bag. That's why it won't happen to me.
I said that at lunch, and Sonali just got up and left. Mrs Pinto, who was on lunch duty, called me over. She said Sonali had been holding her phone to check the bus timing, and that the same bike had snatched from an old man and a lady with a bag that week. "Were they showing off too?" I didn't have an answer.
I think I said it because I'm afraid of it being random.
I'm going to say sorry tomorrow.
Suraj

qa.a: To check the bus timing.

qa.q: Why does Suraj think the blame was said at all?
qa.a: Suraj feels afraid of it being random, so believing Sonali caused it made a snatch seem less likely to happen to Suraj.

qa.q: What does Suraj plan, and why is it right?
qa.a: Saying sorry to Sonali tomorrow, because blaming her added hurt to being robbed.

qa.q: How did Sonali react to Suraj's comment?
qa.a: Sonali got up and left, probably hurt and upset to be blamed after being robbed.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows blaming a robbed classmate to feel safe, until a teacher's facts make the blame collapse.

passage: In Sangli, Himani's phone was snatched at the bus stand on Saturday evening. A boy on a motorbike grabbed it from her hand and was gone. By Monday, the story had gone round Class 11. Deepak, leaning on the classroom door, said loudly, "Well, she was showing it off. What did she expect?" A few boys laughed. Himani was at her desk. She put her head down. Deepak felt a flash of something uncomfortable, then pushed it away. It was her fault, he told himself. If she'd been careful, it wouldn't have happened. And he was careful, so it wouldn't happen to him. At break, the class teacher, who had heard, called Deepak aside. "Himani was holding her phone at a bus stand, like everyone does. Would it be your fault if it were you?" Deepak had no answer.

qa.q: Why did Deepak push away the uncomfortable feeling?

qa.a: The teacher called Deepak aside the same day and asked whether it would be his fault if it happened to him, challenging the blame.

passage: After school in Leeds, Jamal and his friends were talking about Dalia, who had been getting nasty comments online all week. "She posts too much," Jamal said, kicking a stone. "If you put yourself out there, that's what you get." His friends shrugged. Jamal liked that idea. He didn't post much. So it wouldn't happen to him. That evening his older sister showed him something on her phone. Dalia had told her form tutor that morning, and the school had already contacted the parents of the students who'd written the comments. "It's the people writing them who did it, not her," his sister said. "Would you say the same if someone went after you?" Jamal felt his face heat up. He thought about what he'd said at the bus stop, and who had heard.

passage: On Thursday night, Jomon's wallet disappeared from his room in the boys' hostel of the Kottayam school. His door had been open while he showered. At breakfast Harish said, loud enough for everyone, "Leave your door open and cry when things vanish. Your fault, man." Jomon stared at his idli. Harish felt good saying it. If it was Jomon's carelessness, then Harish, who always locked up, was safe. That afternoon the warden called a meeting. Two other rooms had been robbed the same night, and one of them had been locked. "Whoever did this is responsible," the warden said. "Not the boys who lost things." Harish shifted on the bench. His own room was one of the two others. He had been robbed too, and he hadn't even noticed yet.

qa.q: How many other rooms had been robbed the same night?
qa.a: Two other rooms.

qa.q: Why did Harish feel good blaming Jomon at breakfast?
qa.a: It made him feel safe and superior, believing that a careful boy who locked up could not be robbed.

qa.q: How did the warden respond, and why was it important?
qa.a: The warden called a meeting that afternoon and said the thief was responsible, not the boys who lost things, which put the blame where it belonged.

qa.q: What was breakfast like for Jomon?
qa.a: Jomon, already upset about his wallet, was shamed in front of everyone and just stared at his idli.

grounding: Shows a teenager blaming a robbed hostel-mate to feel safe himself, until he learns his own locked room was robbed too.

Okay, Nirmala, you want the real story for the school podcast, so here it is. I'm Pranav, Class 10, and last year I said something I'm not proud of.
A boy on my bus had his bag thrown out of the window by some seniors. Our class teacher found out the same afternoon, called the seniors' parents and sat with him for a long time. And me? I told everyone he must have said something to them first. Like, why else would it happen to him and not me?

qa.a: The sister's question about her own bag made the blame sound plainly unfair, and Pranav chose to sit beside the boy the next morning.

passage:
Monday. Sunaina's blue cycle vanished from outside the town library. In the canteen, Amandeep shrugged. "She probably didn't lock it. Some people are just careless." Saying it made the canteen feel normal again.
Thursday. Amandeep came out after tuition and found his own cycle gone, a cut chain lying on the pavement. He had locked it. He had checked twice. He stood there for a long time, face hot, running through what he might have done wrong and finding nothing.
The next Monday. He found Sunaina on the library steps, waiting for a bus now.
"Did you lock yours?" he asked, and then heard how it sounded. "Sorry. I mean, mine was locked too. I said something stupid about you last week."
Sunaina looked at him for a second. "Yeah. I heard."
"I'm sorry," he said again, and sat down beside her to wait.

qa.q: Where did Sunaina's cycle vanish from?
qa.a: Sunaina's blue cycle vanished from outside the town library.

qa.q: Why did calling Sunaina careless make the canteen 'feel normal again' for Amandeep?
qa.a: Blaming Sunaina let Amandeep feel safe and in control, as if theft only happens to careless people and never to someone like him.

qa.q: What could Amandeep say or do next to repair things with Sunaina?
qa.a: Amandeep could ask how Sunaina is managing without the cycle and offer practical help, and correct the comment with the people who heard it.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel hearing Amandeep's apology?
qa.a: Sunaina may still feel hurt, since she had heard the comment, but the plain admission and his waiting beside her might ease some of the sting.

grounding: Shows a teenager blaming a classmate for a theft to protect his sense of safety, until the same thing happens to him.

passage: Hrithik, you said your friend "asked for it" when those boys took his phone. Sit with me on the steps; the Holi colours can dry. If Sohan had done nothing wrong and still got hurt, then it could happen to me. Blaming him let me feel safe. Sohan heard me. He never walked home with us again.
